Reproducing Bruno, Frost & Humphries (2017) from CRCNS data set apl-1¶

Paper. Bruno AM, Frost WN, Humphries MD (2017). A spiral attractor network drives rhythmic locomotion. eLife 6:e27342. doi:10.7554/elife.27342. The claims file was written from the version of record (PMC5546814): main text, Materials and methods and all figure legends and supplement legends.

Data set. CRCNS apl-1, doi:10.6080/K0SN074B, streamed from the public bucket crcnsarchive under apl-1/live/. Version: unversioned. CRCNS data sets carry no versions (docs/archives.md), and the bucket holds one copy of the processed files (live/; the orig/ folder holds only one raw optical file). That copy is pinned by the MD5 sums printed in the data check, which match the data set's checksums.md5. The paper cites the data set's DOI and no version. Files read: FileTable.mat, SpikeData.mat, ExtracellularData.mat, Coordinates.mat and diode_template.mat; the 6.9 GB raw optical archive is not needed.

Method. The claims file decides what is tested. Where it leaves a detail open, the detail is taken from the paper's Methods or from its code (github.com/mdhumphries/AplysiaAttractorAnalysis at commit e5f28e98), cited in apl.py. Two details recur in almost every claim: the width of the Gaussian kernel and the rule for the number of PCs. Each is run under every reading the criteria list. Where one reading has to be chosen, the adopted reading is own/min80: the median ISI of the recording, after onset, as the kernel SD, and the smallest number of PCs reaching 80% of the variance. This follows the order of the protocol: the Methods first ("at least 80% of the variance"; the median ISI "in population", the recording), then the code (its width, the median ISI, where the printed width cannot give the paper's counts). No single reading makes every claim that depends on it hold; the Summary lists, for each claim whose outcome changes with the reading, the result under each. Outcomes that rest on the choice are marked as assumed in the record.

Revision after verification round 1. The conclusions were restored (the first build left them out); windows count as coalesced and recurrent at at least 90%, as the Methods say; the decoding of fig6d was run under all four readings and the 90% models of fig6s2 with the full history grid; fig7gh was run under all four readings, with participation under each width; fig7s2 was tested with a port of the code's ensemble toolbox; fig1d, fig3a, fig4bc and fig8 gained the outputs the verifier asked for.

Revision after verification round 2. Text the numbers did not support was corrected (the dimension ranges of the printed widths, the consistency of fig4c's means, the exclusion rule in fig7gh); the code's removal rule of fig3h under the adopted reading is now stated; a printout of the decoding forecasts that diverge was added, with a test of their sensitivity to rounding. The record proposes a change of fig6d's outcome to not reproduced, for a third verification round.

Revision after verification round 3. The verifier agreed with the change, and fig6d is now not reproduced. Its conclusion, and fig6s2's, now give the numbers of this execution: the decoding is not exactly the same in every execution (fig6d), and the earlier prose described another one.

import os
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")
os.environ.setdefault("OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS", "1")
import time
import resource
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy import stats

import apl

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)
started = time.time()
D = apl.load()
recs, preps = D["recs"], D["preps"]
print(f"CRCNS data set {apl.DATASET}, version {apl.VERSION}; read {len(D['md5'])} files from {apl.BUCKET} "
      f"in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")

The data set holds 30 recordings, three bouts in each of 10 preparations, in the order of FileTable.mat, which the description says is the paper's numbering. Every neuron id from 1 to N is present in every bout of its preparation, and every neuron spikes after 30 s. The spike files carry no bout number (Bout is empty); the bout is read from the file name (da01, da02, da03). The neuron counts of FileTable.mat match the spike files and the coordinate files. The MD5 sums printed above are the version pinned (CRCNS data sets are not versioned).

# Units, ranges, the clock of the stimulus, and recordings deposited twice.
rows = []
for r in recs:
    t = r["t"]
    pre = np.sum((t >= 25) & (t < 30)) / 5
    stim = np.sum((t >= 30) & (t < 32.5)) / 2.5
    post = np.sum((t >= 32.5) & (t < 37.5)) / 5
    rows.append({"file": r["file"], "pop_rate_25_30": round(pre, 1), "pop_rate_30_32.5": round(stim, 1),
                 "pop_rate_32.5_37.5": round(post, 1)})
clock = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Population spike rate (spikes/s) before, during and after the stimulus at 30 to 32.5 s:")
print(clock.to_string(index=False))
print("Recordings whose rate after 32.5 s exceeds that before 30 s:",
      int((clock["pop_rate_32.5_37.5"] > clock["pop_rate_25_30"]).sum()), "of", len(clock))
# P10 nerve recordings
rows = []
for q in D["p10"]:
    t = q["t"]
    rows.append({"file": q["file"], "prep": q["prep"], "bout": q["bout"], "spikes": t.size,
                 "ids": np.unique(q["ids"]).tolist(), "time_sorted": q["sorted"],
                 "range_s": f"{t.min():.2f} to {t.max():.2f}",
                 "min_interval_ms": round(np.diff(t).min() * 1000, 3),
                 "rate_25_30": round(np.sum((t >= 25) & (t < 30)) / 5, 1),
                 "rate_32.5_37.5": round(np.sum((t >= 32.5) & (t < 37.5)) / 5, 1)})
print("\nP10 recordings:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("Smallest P10 interval as a sampling period: 1 /", round(1 / np.diff(D["p10"][0]["t"]).min(), 1), "Hz")
# duplicate recordings: identical spike trains between any two recordings
sig = {}
for r in recs:
    for i, tr in enumerate(apl.neuron_trains(r)):
        if tr.size > 5:
            sig.setdefault(tuple(np.round(tr, 4)), []).append((r["file"], i + 1))
dup = [v for v in sig.values() if len(v) > 1]
print("\nNeuron spike trains (more than 5 spikes) found identical in two places:", len(dup), dup[:5])
whole = {}
for r in recs:
    whole.setdefault((r["t"].size, round(float(r["t"].sum()), 3)), []).append(r["file"])
print("Recordings with identical spike counts and sums:", [v for v in whole.values() if len(v) > 1])
pd10 = {}
for q in D["p10"]:
    pd10.setdefault((q["t"].size, round(float(q["t"].sum()), 3)), []).append(q["file"])
print("P10 recordings deposited twice:", [v for v in pd10.values() if len(v) > 1])

# Is the P10 nerve on the clock of the population? Cross-correlation of 1 s binned rates after the
# stimulus, against the same with the P10 series shifted by a random amount (circularly).
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
rows = []
for q in D["p10"]:
    r = next(r for r in recs if r["prep"] == q["prep"] and r["bout"] == q["bout"])
    edges = np.arange(33, 122, 0.5)
    pop = np.histogram(r["t"], edges)[0].astype(float)
    nerve = np.histogram(q["t"], edges)[0].astype(float)
    lags = np.arange(-10, 11)
    cc = [np.corrcoef(np.roll(pop, l), nerve)[0, 1] for l in lags]
    shuffled = [np.corrcoef(np.roll(pop, int(rng.integers(20, len(pop) - 20))), nerve)[0, 1] for _ in range(200)]
    rows.append({"file": q["file"], "peak_lag_s": lags[int(np.nanargmax(np.abs(cc)))] * 0.5,
                 "r_at_lag_0": round(cc[10], 3), "max_abs_r": round(np.nanmax(np.abs(cc)), 3),
                 "shifted_95pct_abs_r": round(np.nanpercentile(np.abs(shuffled), 95), 3)})
print("Population rate against P10 rate, 0.5 s bins from 33 s, lags of -5 to 5 s:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
# Are neuron ids the same neurons across bouts? Per-neuron rates after onset, correlated between
# bouts of a preparation, against the same with the ids permuted.
rows = []
for p in range(1, 11):
    rs = [np.array([np.sum(tr >= 30) for tr in apl.neuron_trains(r)]) for r in recs if r["prep"] == p]
    for a, b in apl.PAIRS:
        rho = stats.spearmanr(rs[a], rs[b])[0]
        null = [stats.spearmanr(rs[a], rng.permutation(rs[b]))[0] for _ in range(200)]
        rows.append({"prep": p, "pair": f"{a + 1},{b + 1}", "spearman": round(rho, 3),
                     "permuted_95pct": round(np.percentile(null, 95), 3)})
idt = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("\nRank correlation of neurons' post-onset spike counts between bouts (same id):")
print(idt.pivot(index="prep", columns="pair", values="spearman").to_string())
print("Pairs above the 95th percentile of permuted ids:", int((idt.spearman > idt.permuted_95pct).sum()), "of", len(idt))

Checks of the description against the data. Consistent with the description: 30 recordings, three per preparation; 75 to 160 neurons per preparation, 1131 in all; the stimulus at 30 to 32.5 s (in every recording the population rate during the stimulus exceeds the rate before it, and the rate after 32.5 s exceeds the rate before 30 s in 30 of 30); recordings end at 122.7 s; P10 spikes in nine recordings of preparations 2, 4 and 5 (FileTable lists bouts 1 to 3 for those three). The P10 intervals are multiples of 0.614 ms, a sampling rate of 1629.7 Hz, which agrees with the description's 1630 Hz and not with the paper's 1600 Hz. The P10 files of preparation 2 are named Jun0414, its spike file Jun0414B; they are matched on the first seven characters, as the code does. No neuron spike train and no recording appears twice.

The P10 rate and the population rate are correlated after the stimulus at lags of 0 to 5 s in every P10 recording; in 7 of 9 the largest correlation exceeds the 95th percentile of circularly shifted series. This is consistent with a shared clock; the lag of a few seconds is expected for a nerve that fires in one phase of a 10 s cycle, so it does not show the clocks agree to better than a few seconds. In Jun1114da01 and Jun1114da02 the check does not separate the data from shifted series.

The description says the recordings were concatenated before spike sorting, so that a neuron id names the same neuron in all three bouts. Consistent with this, per-neuron spike counts after onset correlate between bouts of a preparation (Spearman 0.63 to 0.96) above the 95th percentile of permuted ids in 30 of 30 pairs. This is taken as an assumption for the participation claims, which compare neurons across bouts; their results are given per preparation and bout.

Coordinates hold one (x, y) per neuron, on a 0 to 50 scale (plot_maps.m multiplies by 10 to plot them on the 501 by 501 diode template). Preparations 7 and 8 are marked unreliable, as the description says, and preparation 7 has 5 missing positions. No unit is given, and nothing in the files or the documentation says which direction of x or y is rostral, caudal, medial or lateral.

dataset-size¶

Three bouts of fictive locomotion were evoked in each of 10 isolated preparations (30 population responses); each recorded population held 120 to 180 neurons, 1131 neurons in all.

In [8]:
# Variant (not judged): is the low-frequency peak the slow decay of the rate (claim fig1e) or an
# oscillation? The population rate from stimulation offset in 0.1 s bins, minus a quadratic fit in
# time (the decay), with a multitaper spectrum (DPSS, time-bandwidth 3, 5 tapers, as the main
# spectrum). Reported: the frequency of maximum power above 0.02 Hz, the code's weighted peak, and
# the power in 0.05 to 0.11 Hz relative to 0.2 to 1 Hz.
from scipy.signal.windows import dpss
rows = []
for r in recs:
    edges = np.arange(apl.STIM_OFF, r["t"].max(), 0.1)
    y = np.histogram(r["t"], edges)[0].astype(float) / 0.1
    tt = edges[:-1] + 0.05
    y_d = y - np.polyval(np.polyfit(tt, y, 2), tt)
    tp = dpss(y.size, 3, 5)
    nfft = int(2 ** np.ceil(np.log2(y.size)) * 2)
    fr = np.fft.rfftfreq(nfft, 0.1)
    Sd = np.mean(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(tp * y_d, nfft)) ** 2, 0)
    keep = (fr > 0) & (fr <= 1)
    fk, Sk = fr[keep], Sd[keep]
    band = Sk[(fk >= 0.05) & (fk <= 0.11)].mean() / Sk[(fk >= 0.2) & (fk <= 1)].mean()
    above = fk > 0.02
    rows.append({"file": r["file"], "fmax_detrended": fk[above][np.argmax(Sk[above])], "weighted_peak_detrended": apl.peak_frequency(fk, Sk),
                 "band_ratio_0.05-0.11_vs_0.2-1": band})
DT1 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"frequency grid step {fk[1] - fk[0]:.4f} Hz")
print("detrended population rate, frequency of maximum power above 0.02 Hz: min", round(DT1.fmax_detrended.min(), 4), "median",
      round(DT1.fmax_detrended.median(), 4), "max", round(DT1.fmax_detrended.max(), 4), "; at or below 0.11 Hz:",
      int((DT1.fmax_detrended <= 0.11).sum()), "of 30")
print("weighted peak of the detrended spectrum: min", round(DT1.weighted_peak_detrended.min(), 4), "median",
      round(DT1.weighted_peak_detrended.median(), 4), "max", round(DT1.weighted_peak_detrended.max(), 4), "; at or below 0.11 Hz:",
      int((DT1.weighted_peak_detrended <= 0.11).sum()), "of 30")
print("mean power 0.05 to 0.11 Hz over mean power 0.2 to 1 Hz: min", round(DT1["band_ratio_0.05-0.11_vs_0.2-1"].min(), 1), "median",
      round(DT1["band_ratio_0.05-0.11_vs_0.2-1"].median(), 1), "; above 1 in", int((DT1["band_ratio_0.05-0.11_vs_0.2-1"] > 1).sum()), "of 30")
print("grand mean point-process spectrum at its first bins (Hz: power):", {round(float(a), 4): round(float(b), 3) for a, b in zip(f[1:8], grand[1:8])})

Result: reproduced. The grand mean spectrum's power-weighted peak is at 0.0486 Hz, and the peaks of all 30 recordings lie above 0 and at or below 0.11 Hz (0.0131 to 0.0789 Hz). The variant, the frequency of maximum power above 0 Hz, lies at 0.0076 to 0.0992 Hz, also 30 of 30 at or below 0.11 Hz. A detrended check, not judged, tells the oscillation from the decay of the rate (claim fig1e): with a quadratic trend removed from the population rate after offset, the frequency of maximum power above 0.02 Hz is 0.034 to 0.156 Hz (median 0.064 Hz), at or below 0.11 Hz in 27 of 30, and the mean power in 0.05 to 0.11 Hz exceeds that in 0.2 to 1 Hz in 30 of 30 (median ratio 9.8). The grand mean point-process spectrum is nearly flat over its first bins (7.54 at 0.0076 Hz, 7.24 at 0.053 Hz), so its maximum at the lowest bin reflects the decay as well as the oscillation.

fig1e-decaying-rate¶

The population firing rate decays slowly after the stimulus, decreasing in most evoked responses.

In [9]:
rows = []
for r in recs:
    t = r["t"]
    starts = np.arange(30, r["t"].max() - 20 + 1e-9, 5)
    counts = np.array([np.sum((t >= s) & (t < s + 20)) for s in starts])
    R = np.corrcoef(starts + 10, counts)[0, 1]
    edges = np.arange(32.5, r["t"].max(), 1.0)
    rate = np.histogram(t, edges)[0]
    slope = np.polyfit(edges[:-1] + 0.5, rate, 1)[0]
    rows.append({"prep": r["prep"], "bout": r["bout"], "R_20s_windows": R, "n_windows": len(starts), "slope_spikes_per_s2": slope})
rate_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)

fig2b-dimensions¶

Capturing 80% of the population variance needs 4 to 8 embedding dimensions in the evoked responses, a reduction by more than a factor of 10 from the number of neurons.

The Gaussian SD is read four ways (helper docstring) and the count two ways, as the criterion lists them.

Result: reproduced, under the readings with the code's width and the code's count. The criterion asks for one reading. With the median ISI as the SD and the count of PCs whose cumulative variance is at most 80% (own/le80), 28 of 30 counts lie in 3.6 to 8.8 (3 to 7) and the number of neurons divided by the count exceeds 10 in all 30 (lowest 10.7); pooled/le80 gives the same. With the Methods' count (smallest number reaching 80%) the counts are 4 to 8 for own/min80, the paper's range, all 30 in 3.6 to 8.8, but the ratio exceeds 10 in 29 of 30 (lowest 9.4, 75 neurons and 8 PCs). The Methods' printed width gives 21 to 76 dimensions (median ISI / sqrt(12), 21 to 41; median ISI / 12, 33 to 76) and ratios of 1.8 to 2.8 at the lowest; it cannot give the paper's counts. The adopted reading of the later claims (own/min80) is therefore one under which this claim fails, by one response; its counts are the paper's 4 to 8.

The recurrence analysis¶

Run once per reading of the width and the count. The local linear models (claims fig4 to fig5) are fitted for the four readings with the code's width; the two narrow widths give 21 to 76 dimensions (claim fig2b-dimensions) and are carried only through the dominant period (fig2ef-periodic-recurrence). The adopted reading, used where one reading has to be chosen, is own/min80: the median ISI of the recording (the width the code uses; the Methods compute it "in population", the recording) and the smallest number of PCs reaching 80% (the Methods, "at least 80% of the variance"). The other readings are shown with it.

No single reading makes every claim that depends on it hold. Under the adopted reading claim fig2b fails by one response (75 neurons over 8 PCs, a ratio of 9.4), though its counts are the paper's 4 to 8; own/le80 passes fig2b, fig3h and fig6s2 but gives a linear-model period of 13.55 s for fig4c. The Summary tabulates the outcome under each reading for the claims that change.

In [11]:
t0 = time.time()
RUNS = {}
for mode in ["own", "pooled"]:
    for rule in ["min80", "le80"]:
        RUNS[f"{mode}/{rule}"] = apl.run_all(recs, sds[mode], rule, lld=True, workers=4)
for mode in ["sqrt12", "twelve"]:
    for rule in ["min80", "le80"]:
        RUNS[f"{mode}/{rule}"] = apl.run_all(recs, sds[mode], rule, lld=False, workers=4)
SUM = {k: pd.DataFrame([apl.summarise(o) for o in v]) for k, v in RUNS.items()}
print(f"recurrence analysis of 30 recordings under {len(RUNS)} readings in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; "
      f"peak memory {resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN).ru_maxrss / 1e6:.2f} GB per worker")

fig2ef-periodic-recurrence¶

The evoked low-dimensional activity recurs with a regular period; strongly periodic recurrence on the scale of 10 to 15 s is found in many but not all of the 30 responses.

fig2s2-threshold-robust¶

The periodic orbits are robust to the threshold for recurrence, with similar periodicity at thresholds of 10%, 5% and 2%.

In [14]:
rows = []
for k in ["own/min80", "own/le80", "pooled/min80", "pooled/le80"]:
    P = {th: pd.DataFrame([apl.summarise(o, i) for o in RUNS[k]]) for i, th in enumerate(apl.THETA_PRCT)}
    for stat in ["period_mean", "period_median"]:
        p10 = P[10][stat].values
        for th in (5, 2):
            pl = P[th][stat].values
            ok = np.isfinite(p10) & np.isfinite(pl)
            rho, p = stats.spearmanr(p10[ok], pl[ok])
            mad = np.median(np.abs(pl[ok] - p10[ok]))
            rows.append({"reading": k, "period": stat, "theta": f"{th}%", "n_both": int(ok.sum()),
                         "spearman": round(rho, 3), "p": p, "(a)": bool(rho > 0 and p < 0.05),
                         "median_abs_diff_s": round(mad, 2), "10pct_of_median": round(0.1 * np.median(p10[ok]), 2),
                         "(b)": bool(mad < 0.1 * np.median(p10[ok]))})

fig3a-coalescence¶

Almost all evoked responses reach a state of high recurrence within one oscillation period of stimulation and are thereafter dominated by recurrence.

The coalescence time is the mid-point of the first 5 s window with at least 90% recurrent points (Methods). Windows start at 35 s, where the checked points start (Methods), so the earliest possible value is 37.5 s, 7.5 s after onset.

plotted: the first six responses, densities 0 to 1

Result: not reproduced. Under the adopted reading, the coalescence time (first window with at least 90% recurrent points) is within one dominant period of stimulation onset in 12 of 30 responses (19 of 30 measured from offset), where the criterion asks for 27; the other readings give 11 to 14 (17 to 20 from offset). Coalescence comes 7.5 to 49.5 s after onset (median 14.5 s). The second part holds: after coalescence more than 50% of the points recur in 30 of 30 responses (60.8% to 98.6%, median 86%). Because the checked points start at 35 s, the earliest possible coalescence is 7.5 s after onset, close to the shortest periods (8.7 to 9.4 s). The late coalescence is not an edge effect of the 90% line: within one period of onset the highest window density reaches 0.8 in 15 of 30 responses and 0.7 in 21.

Comparisons between the programs of a preparation¶

Hausdorff distances on the axes of program 1 (claim fig3c) and on common axes (fig3s1a), with 100 neuron shuffles each way as control; the distances of Figure 3D; the similarity matrices of Figure 3F. Run for the four readings with the code's width (the point sets come from each reading's recurrence analysis).

In [17]:
t0 = time.time()
MAN = {k: apl.run_manifold(recs, sds[k.split("/")[0]], RUNS[k], n_shuffle=100, seed=1)
       for k in ["own/min80", "own/le80", "pooled/min80", "pooled/le80"]}
print(f"comparisons in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
def haus_table(k, axes, ps):
    rows = []
    for m in MAN[k]:
        for (i, j) in apl.PAIRS:
            h, c = m[(axes, ps, i, j)]
            rows.append({"prep": m["prep"], "pair": f"{i + 1},{j + 1}", "H": h, "ctrl_mean": np.mean(c),
                         "ctrl_2sem": 2 * np.std(c, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(c.size), "dims": m["k_prog1" if axes == "prog1" else "k_common"]})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

comparisons in 137 s

fig3c-same-manifold¶

Sequentially evoked responses of a preparation fall on the same manifold; their distance is below that of random projections for all pairs except two, pairs (1,2) and (1,3) of preparation 4.

In [18]:
rows = []
for k in MAN:
    for ps in ["recurrent", "code"]:
        T = haus_table(k, "prog1", ps)
        below = T.H < T.ctrl_mean
        rows.append({"reading": k, "points": ps, "pairs_below_control": int(below.sum()),
                     "failing_pairs": [(p, q) for p, q in zip(T.prep[~below], T.pair[~below])]})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
T = haus_table(ADOPT, "prog1", "recurrent")
print("\nadopted reading, recurrent points:")

Result: reproduced. With the code's point sets, 28 of 30 pairs are closer than their random-projection control under every reading, and the two that fail are pairs (1,2) and (1,3) of preparation 4, as the paper names them (distance 1.19 and 1.17 times the control under the adopted reading). With the recurrent points (the Methods), 29 of 30 pass under every reading and only pair (1,2) of preparation 4 fails (1.04 times the control). The control's 2 s.e.m. is 0.11 to 0.36, small against the differences.

fig3d-initial-conditions¶

Stimulation drives responses of the same preparation far apart before coalescence, more than at stimulus onset or after both have coalesced, so the same manifold is reached from different initial conditions.

The transient distance is the largest distance between a point of one program and a point of the other between onset and their coalescence; for speed every fifth point of the second program is used (a standard choice: neighbouring points 10 ms apart are nearly equal).

In [20]:

                             "onset": on, "transient": tr, "coalesced": m[("common", ps, i, j)][0]})

fig3f-pairwise-similarity¶

Pairwise similarity between neurons is preserved across responses of the same preparation, above a null model, except for pairs (1,3) and (2,3) of preparation 7.

In [21]:
rows, detail = [], []
for k in MAN:
    for meth in ["spearman", "pearson"]:
        corr = (lambda a, b: stats.spearmanr(a, b)[0]) if meth == "spearman" else (lambda a, b: np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1])
        for ctl in ["first", "larger"]:
            n, fails = 0, []
            for m in MAN[k]:
                Sm, Em = m["sim"]
                cs = [corr(Sm[i].ravel(), Em[i].ravel()) for i in range(3)]
                for (i, j) in apl.PAIRS:
                    dat = corr(Sm[i].ravel(), Sm[j].ravel())
                    c = cs[i] if ctl == "first" else max(cs[i], cs[j])
                    if dat > c:
                        n += 1
                    else:
                        fails.append((m["prep"], f"{i + 1},{j + 1}"))
                    if k == ADOPT and ctl == "first":
                        detail.append({"corr": meth, "prep": m["prep"], "pair": f"{i + 1},{j + 1}", "data": dat,
                                       "control_first": cs[i], "control_second": cs[j]})
            rows.append({"reading": k, "corr": meth, "control": ctl, "pairs_above": n, "failing": fails})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("\nadopted reading:")
print(pd.DataFrame(detail).round(3).to_string(index=False))

fig3h-perturbations-return¶

Of 19 spontaneous divergences from the trajectory, 17 (90%) returned to a recurrent state; the two that did not were consistent with the end of the evoked locomotion.

A divergent period (Methods) is a run of windows after coalescence with recurrence density below 90% that falls below 50%; "returned" means a later window is above 90%. Periods whose divergent point lies within two dominant periods of the end are removed (Methods), with the dominant period read as the mean or the median of the peak. The code removes only periods that never return (Are_jumps_perturbations_or_transitions2.m); that is shown as a variant.

In [22]:
DIV = {}
rows = []
for k in ["own/min80", "own/le80", "pooled/min80", "pooled/le80"]:
    for stat in ["period_mean", "period_median"]:
        allv = []
        for o, s in zip(RUNS[k], SUM[k].itertuples()):
            for d in apl.divergences(o, getattr(s, stat)):
                d.update(prep=o["prep"], bout=o["bout"])
                allv.append(d)
        V = pd.DataFrame(allv)
        DIV[(k, stat)] = V
        kept = V[~V.near_end]
        code_kept = V[V.returned | ~V.near_end]
        rows.append({"reading": k, "period": stat, "all_periods": len(V), "kept": len(kept),
                     "returned": int(kept.returned.sum()), "fraction": round(kept.returned.mean(), 3),
                     "code_rule_kept": len(code_kept), "code_rule_returned": int(code_kept.returned.sum())})

Result: partially reproduced, resting on the adopted reading. Under the adopted reading with the Methods' period (mean of the dominant peak), 34 divergent periods are found and 16 remain after removing those within two periods of the end; 15 of 16 (0.938) returned above 90%. The fraction matches (at least 80%), but both counts fall just short of their tolerances: 16 divergent periods against 17.1 to 20.9, and 15 returns against 15.3 to 18.7. With the median period (the code's) 17 remain and 16 return (0.941); 16 returns are within tolerance, but 17 periods are just below 17.1. Over the four readings 14 to 19 periods remain and 13 to 17 return, 0.875 to 0.941. The code's rule (dropping only the periods within two cycles of the end that never return) keeps 17 to 21 over the readings, and under the adopted reading it keeps 19 periods of which 18 return (0.947), with either period, which meets both tolerances and matches the paper's 19. The criterion states the Methods' rule ("We removed all such divergent periods whose divergent point fell within two oscillation cycles of the end of the recording", Testing return to the same manifold after perturbation), so the code's rule is reported, not judged. Under the Methods' rule the counts meet the criterion only under own/le80, with either period (18 kept and 16 returned; 19 and 17). With eight combinations run, a pass under one of them is weak evidence, and the adopted reading's result decides. The criterion has no partial outcome; it is recorded as partially reproduced because the returned fraction holds and the two counts miss their tolerances by 1.1 and 0.3.

fig4bc-stable-spiral¶

The evoked responses have highly clustered maximum eigenvalues of the local linear dynamics, dominated by negative complex values, so the pedal ganglion implements a contracting periodic orbit, a stable spiral attractor, found in every preparation.

Result: reproduced, resting on the adopted reading. The mean over the 30 responses of 2 pi / b times 0.01 s is 10.45 s under the adopted reading (9 to 11 s required); the variant, the mean of the per-point rotation periods, is 10.24 s. Under the code's count rule the means are 13.55 s (own/le80) and 12.22 s (pooled/le80), outside the tolerance. The per-response linear periods do not correlate with the recurrence periods (Pearson r = -0.063, p = 0.74, adopted; -0.12 to 0.03 for the other readings), and the means do not agree within the claim's tolerance either: 10.45 s against a median recurrence period of 12.73 s, 2.3 s apart where the tolerance is 1 s. The criterion judges the mean against 10 s and reports the correlation, so the statement's "consistent with" is reported, not judged; neither the correlation nor the means support it.

fig5b-period-changes¶

Over a response the orbital period may slow, speed up or not change; all three occur among the 30 responses.

In [28]:
t0 = time.time()
PC = {}
rows = []
for k in ["own/min80", "pooled/le80", "own/le80", "pooled/min80"]:
    out = []
    for n, o in enumerate(RUNS[k]):
        w = o["windows"][-1]
        hi = np.flatnonzero(w["dens"] >= 0.9)
        sl = slice(hi[0], hi[-1] + 1)
        wt = 1 / w["sddelay"]
        wt[~np.isfinite(wt)] = 0
        wt = wt * w["dens"]
        r, p, nw = apl.weighted_spearman(w["mid_t"][sl], w["mdelay"][sl], wt[sl], 10000, np.random.default_rng(500 + n))
        row = {"prep": o["prep"], "bout": o["bout"], "rho": r, "p": p, "n_windows": nw}
        if k == ADOPT:
            rc, pcode, _ = apl.weighted_spearman(w["mid_t"][sl], w["mdelay"][sl], wt[sl], 100000, np.random.default_rng(900 + n), pooled=True)
            row.update(p_code=pcode)
        out.append(row)
    X = pd.DataFrame(out)
    PC[k] = X
    rows.append({"reading": k, "slowing_p<0.01": int(((X.rho > 0) & (X.p < 0.01)).sum()),
                 "speeding_p<0.01": int(((X.rho < 0) & (X.p < 0.01)).sum()), "no_change": int((X.p >= 0.01).sum()),
                 "windows_min": X.n_windows.min(), "windows_max": X.n_windows.max()})
print(f"permutation tests in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced. Under the adopted reading, 12 responses slow (rho > 0, p < 0.01), 4 speed up (rho < 0, p < 0.01) and 14 do not change at that level; the code's pooled one-sided test gives 13, 4 and 13. The number of windows per response is 31 to 73, within 27.9 to 79.2. The other readings give 10 to 14 slowing, 4 to 6 speeding and 11 to 15 unchanged. The windows used run from the first to the last window with at least 90% recurrent points.

fig5c-no-relation-contraction¶

There is no relationship between the change in orbital period over a response and its rate of contraction, as a stable spiral predicts.

In [29]:
rows = []
for k, X in PC.items():
    E = EIG[k]
    r, p = stats.pearsonr(X.rho, E.a)
    contraction = np.exp(100 * E.a) * 100 - 100
    r2, p2 = stats.pearsonr(X.rho, contraction)
    rows.append({"reading": k, "R_rho_vs_a": r, "p": p, "R_rho_vs_contraction_pct": r2, "p_contraction": p2})

Result: reproduced. Across the 30 responses, Pearson's R between the weighted rho and the mean real part of the maximum eigenvalue is -0.341 (p = 0.065) under the adopted reading, and -0.342 (p = 0.064) with the contraction in %/s. The other readings give R = -0.14 to -0.34 (p = 0.064 to 0.46). The test does not find the relation at p < 0.05, but the effect is moderate and p is close to the threshold under two readings.

fig6s1-no-p10-motorneurons¶

No recorded neuron is a P10 motorneuron; no neuron comes close to one-to-one locking of its spikes with P10 spikes at any delay, nor locks consistently across programs.

fig6d-decode-p10¶

P10 nerve activity can be fitted and forecast from the low-dimensional trajectory in all nine responses with P10 recordings, so the trajectory encodes muscle commands.

Adopted width (median ISI of the recording); PCs for 80% (smallest number reaching it). The Methods' windowing (fit 40 s, forecast 10 s, step 1 s, from 33 s; histories 50 to 200 ms) is the main reading; the code's (training on 50% of the series, 0.2 s steps, histories 50 to 250 ms) is a variant. Every reading of width and count is run with the Methods' windowing. The 90% models of claim fig6s2 use the Methods' windowing with the full history grid under own/min80 and own/le80, and with histories of 50, 100, 150 and 200 ms under pooled/le80, to fit the time limit.

In [31]:
t0 = time.time()
def p10_jobs(frac, windowing, hists, mode="own", rule="min80"):
    J = []
    for q in D["p10"]:
        i = next(i for i, r in enumerate(recs) if r["prep"] == q["prep"] and r["bout"] == q["bout"])
        J.append((recs[i], q["t"], float(sds[mode][i]), frac, windowing, hists, rule))
    return J
DEC = {("own/min80", "80", "methods"): apl.run_decoding(p10_jobs(0.8, "methods", apl.HISTORIES_METHODS)),
       ("own/min80", "80", "code"): apl.run_decoding(p10_jobs(0.8, "code", apl.HISTORIES_CODE)),
       ("own/min80", "90", "methods"): apl.run_decoding(p10_jobs(0.9, "methods", apl.HISTORIES_METHODS))}
for k in ["own/le80", "pooled/min80", "pooled/le80"]:
    mode, rule = k.split("/")
    DEC[(k, "80", "methods")] = apl.run_decoding(p10_jobs(0.8, "methods", apl.HISTORIES_METHODS, mode, rule))
# 90% models for claim fig6s2: the full history grid under the two readings with the recording's own
# width; under pooled/le80 four histories only (50 to 200 ms in 50 ms steps), to fit the time limit.
DEC[("own/le80", "90", "methods")] = apl.run_decoding(p10_jobs(0.9, "methods", apl.HISTORIES_METHODS, "own", "le80"))
DEC[("pooled/le80", "90", "methods")] = apl.run_decoding(p10_jobs(0.9, "methods", [5, 10, 15, 20], "pooled", "le80"))
print(f"decoding in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
def dec_table(res, hists=None):
    rows = []
    for o in res:
        if hists is None:
            R = np.array([w["R"] for w in o["windows"]]); MAE = np.array([w["MAE"] for w in o["windows"]]); best = o["best"]
        else:
            best = min(hists, key=lambda h: np.nanmean(o["by_history"][h][1]))
            R, MAE = o["by_history"][best]
        ok = np.isfinite(R)
        sem = np.nanstd(R, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(ok.sum())
        rows.append({"prep": o["prep"], "bout": o["bout"], "dims": o["d"], "history_ms": best * 10, "windows": len(R),
                     "undefined_R": int((~ok).sum()), "mean_R": np.nanmean(R), "mean_R_minus_2sem": np.nanmean(R) - 2 * sem,
                     "mean_R2": np.nanmean(R ** 2), "mean_MAE": np.nanmean(MAE),
                     "train_R": np.nanmean([w["R_train"] for w in o["windows"]]) if hists is None else np.nan})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
for name, res, h in [("own/min80, Methods windowing, 80%", DEC[("own/min80", "80", "methods")], None),
                     ("own/min80, variant: histories up to 100 ms", DEC[("own/min80", "80", "methods")], list(range(5, 11))),
                     ("own/min80, variant: code windowing", DEC[("own/min80", "80", "code")], None)]:
    T = dec_table(res, h)
    print(f"\n{name}: responses with mean R - 2 s.e.m. > 0: {int((T.mean_R_minus_2sem > 0).sum())} of 9; windows in all {T.windows.sum()}")
    print(T.round(3).to_string(index=False))
rows = []
for k in ["own/min80", "own/le80", "pooled/min80", "pooled/le80"]:
    for name, h in [("Methods", None), ("up to 100 ms", list(range(5, 11)))]:
        T = dec_table(DEC[(k, "80", "methods")], h)
        f = T[(T.prep == 4) & (T.bout == 1)].iloc[0]
        rows.append({"reading": k, "histories": name, "dims": T.dims.tolist(), "pass": int((T.mean_R_minus_2sem > 0).sum()),
                     "mean_R_min": T.mean_R.min(), "mean_R_max": T.mean_R.max(),
                     "prep4_bout1_mean_R": f.mean_R, "prep4_bout1_bound": f.mean_R_minus_2sem})
print("\nevery reading of width and count, Methods windowing (responses passing of 9):")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))

# Preparation 4, bout 1 against a response that decodes well (preparation 4, bout 2): the P10 rate and
# the forecast of four of the Methods' windows, adopted reading and each program's best history.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 5), sharex=True)
for ax, bout in zip(axes, [1, 2]):
    q = next(q for q in D["p10"] if q["prep"] == 4 and q["bout"] == bout)
    i = next(i for i, r in enumerate(recs) if r["prep"] == 4 and r["bout"] == bout)
    o = next(o for o in DEC[("own/min80", "80", "methods")] if o["prep"] == 4 and o["bout"] == bout)
    P = apl.Program(recs[i], float(sds["own"][i]))
    pcs = P.proj[:, :o["d"]]
    rate = apl.sdf_matrix([q["t"]], float(sds["own"][i]), P.t_end)[P.ix_stim, 0]
    h = o["best"]
    ax.plot(P.stimbins, rate, color="0.6", lw=0.8, label="P10 rate")
    for s0 in [33.0, 43.0, 53.0, 63.0]:
        i0, i1 = np.searchsorted(P.stimbins, s0 - 1e-9), np.searchsorted(P.stimbins, s0 + 40 - 1e-9)
        rows_ = np.arange(max(i0, h), i1)
        b = apl.poisson_glm(apl.lagged(pcs, rows_, h), rate[rows_])
        rf = np.arange(i1, min(i1 + 1000, rate.size))
        fc = np.exp(np.clip(apl.lagged(pcs, rf, h) @ b, -30, 30))
        ax.plot(P.stimbins[rf], fc, lw=1, label=f"forecast after fit from {s0:.0f} s")
        print(f"prep 4 bout {bout}, window from {s0:.0f} s: forecast R {np.corrcoef(rate[rf], fc)[0, 1]:.3f}; "
              f"P10 rate range {rate[rf].min():.1f} to {rate[rf].max():.1f}, forecast range {fc.min():.1f} to {fc.max():.1f} spikes/s")
    ax.set_ylabel("spikes/s"); ax.set_title(f"preparation 4, bout {bout}"); ax.set_ylim(0, np.percentile(rate, 99.5) * 1.5)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, ncol=3); axes[1].set_xlabel("time (s)"); axes[1].set_xlim(70, 120)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Diverging forecasts: windows whose largest forecast exceeds 10 times the response's largest P10
# rate (reported, not judged). The linear predictor is clipped at 30, so a diverging forecast reaches
# about 1e13 spikes/s, and a few such windows dominate a mean MAE over windows.
def diverging(res, frac_label):
    rows = []
    for o in res:
        lim = 10 * o["rate_max"]
        allh = np.concatenate(list(o["fc_max_by_history"].values()))
        sel = o["fc_max_by_history"][o["best"]]
        rows.append({"model": frac_label, "prep": o["prep"], "bout": o["bout"], "history_ms": o["best"] * 10,
                     "diverging_selected": int((sel > lim).sum()), "windows": sel.size,
                     "largest_forecast_selected": sel.max(), "diverging_all_histories": int((allh > lim).sum()),
                     "windows_all_histories": allh.size})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
rows = []
for key, res in DEC.items():
    T = diverging(res, "/".join(key))
    rows.append({"reading": key[0], "variance": key[1], "windowing": key[2],
                 "responses_with_diverging_selected": int((T.diverging_selected > 0).sum()),
                 "diverging_selected": int(T.diverging_selected.sum()), "windows_selected": int(T.windows.sum()),
                 "largest_forecast_selected": T.largest_forecast_selected.max(),
                 "diverging_all_histories": int(T.diverging_all_histories.sum()),
                 "windows_all_histories": int(T.windows_all_histories.sum())})
print("windows with a forecast above 10 times the response's largest P10 rate, per decoding run:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("\nown/min80, code windowing, 80%, per response:")
print(diverging(DEC[("own/min80", "80", "code")], "code").to_string(index=False))

# Sensitivity to rounding: preparation 4, bout 1, own/min80, code windowing, with the PCs perturbed
# by Gaussian noise of 1e-9 times their SD (seeded).
rng_div = np.random.default_rng(611)
i41 = next(i for i, r in enumerate(recs) if r["prep"] == 4 and r["bout"] == 1)
q41 = next(q for q in D["p10"] if q["prep"] == 4 and q["bout"] == 1)
P41 = apl.Program(recs[i41], float(sds["own"][i41]), "min80")
pcs41 = P41.proj[:, :apl.n_pcs(P41.ev, 0.8, "min80")]
rate41 = apl.sdf_matrix([q41["t"]], float(sds["own"][i41]), P41.t_end)[P41.ix_stim, 0]
rows = []
for h in [5, 15]:
    for name, X in [("as computed", pcs41), ("perturbed 1e-9 SD", pcs41 + 1e-9 * pcs41.std(0) * rng_div.standard_normal(pcs41.shape))]:
        o = apl.decode_p10(X, rate41, P41.stimbins, h, step_s=0.2, train_frac=0.5)
        M = np.array([w["MAE"] for w in o]); R = np.array([w["R"] for w in o]); F = np.array([w["fc_max"] for w in o])
        rows.append({"history_ms": h * 10, "pcs": name, "mean_MAE": M.mean(), "median_MAE": np.median(M),
                     "mean_R": np.nanmean(R), "diverging": int((F > 10 * rate41.max()).sum()), "windows": len(o)})
print("\npreparation 4, bout 1, own/min80, code windowing, sensitivity to a perturbation of the PCs:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Result: not reproduced. With the Methods' windowing, 8 of 9 responses have mean forecast R minus 2 s.e.m. above 0 under every reading of width and count (adopted: mean R of the other eight 0.36 to 0.89). Response 1 of preparation 4 fails under all four readings (mean R -0.060, -0.120, -0.080 and -0.123 for own/min80, own/le80, pooled/min80 and pooled/le80; bounds -0.127 to -0.204), with histories up to 100 ms and with the code's windowing (mean R -0.102, bound -0.131). Its training fits are as good as the others' (mean training R 0.94; 0.91 to 0.97 in all nine), but its forecasts fail: in the four windows plotted the forecast R is -0.59 to 0.27, and the first forecast runs at 56 to 133 spikes/s against a P10 rate of 0 to 24 spikes/s, while response 2 of the same preparation gives 0.81 to 0.94. The decoding holds in eight of nine responses. The criterion requires it in each of the nine, the statement says "in all nine", and the one failure holds under every reading, history range and windowing run here, so the result is a failure of what the claim says. Verification round 3 agreed with the change from partially reproduced. The Methods' windowing gives 40 forecast windows per response (360 in all), the code's 174 per response (1566); the paper's N = 173 is close to the code's count per response. Preparation 4's first response is the one the paper describes as apparently chaotic (Figure 3, figure supplement 1B).

The decoding does not give the same numbers in every execution, as the forecasts diverge in some windows and the selected history and the means over windows follow them. The numbers above and below are from this execution. The copy reviewed in verification round 3 gave mean R -0.060, -0.127, -0.060 and -0.119 for preparation 4, bout 1 (bounds -0.128 to -0.206) and -0.101 with the code's windowing, and the same 8 of 9 under every reading; the pass counts have been the same in every execution.

Here, over all histories, 462 to 627 of 5760 windows (80% models, Methods windowing, the four readings) and 1614 of 7830 (code windowing) have a forecast above 10 times the response's largest P10 rate, up to the clip of the linear predictor (about 1e13 spikes/s). Of the histories selected for the 80% models, one window diverges, under pooled/min80 (largest forecast 1.2e9 spikes/s); the other 80% runs have none (largest forecast 338 to 660 spikes/s). For preparation 4, bout 1 with the code's windowing, perturbing the PCs by 1e-9 of their SD leaves the 50 ms model nearly unchanged (mean MAE 13.27 and 13.32, mean R -0.102 and -0.101, no diverging window) but changes the 150 ms model's mean MAE from 5.3e11 to 4.2e11 (74 and 78 diverging windows of 174). A mean MAE over windows with diverging forecasts therefore depends on rounding, and so can the history selected: the copy reviewed in round 3 selected a history for this response with a mean MAE of 7.6e6, where this execution's has 13.3. The forecast R of the selected models, on which the criterion rests, moves by up to 0.02 between executions and the failure of this response holds in each.

fig6s2-dimensions-p10¶

The nine recordings with P10 activity need only 3 to 5 embedding dimensions for 80% variance, and at least double that for 90%; using the 90% dimensions does not improve the P10 forecasts.

Result: reproduced, under own/le80. Under the readings with the code's count rule the nine 80% counts lie in 3 to 5 (own/le80: 3 to 5; pooled/le80: 3 to 5), and the 90% counts are at least twice them in each. Under own/le80, with the full history grid for both, the 90% models are not better: mean MAE lower with 90% in 5 of 9 (two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.91, median difference -0.13) and mean R-squared higher in 4 of 9 (p = 0.50, median difference -0.008). So one reading shows both parts. Under pooled/le80 (four histories) the 90% models are not better either (p = 0.65 and 0.82). Under the adopted reading (own/min80) the counts are 4 to 6, and one (6) is outside 2.7 to 5.5; there the 90% models are worse in MAE (p = 0.027, 7 of 9 worse, median +1.23 with the full grid; p = 0.020 with four histories for both) and do not differ in R-squared (p = 0.13). No test finds the 90% models better at p < 0.05 in any of the five comparisons. Of the selected 90% models one, two and two windows diverge under own/min80, own/le80 and pooled/le80 (largest forecast 2.5e6, 1.4e7 and 8.1e8 spikes/s), and over all histories 1166 and 1111 of 5760 windows diverge under own/min80 and own/le80 (fig6d's printout), so the mean MAEs and these p-values depend on rounding through the history selected and differ between executions: this execution gives the numbers above, and earlier executions gave p = 0.50 and 0.91 for MAE under own/le80, with the same conclusion each time.

Participation¶

Per program, from its own PCA under the adopted width; d is (a) the program's own count for 80% (Methods) or (b) the count from the PCA of the three programs concatenated, at most 80%, used for all three (code). Normalised to the program's maximum.

In [35]:
progs = [apl.Program(r, s, "min80") for r, s in zip(recs, sds["own"])]
PART = {}
for reading in ["a_own", "b_common"]:
    for p in range(1, 11):
        ix = sorted([i for i, r in enumerate(recs) if r["prep"] == p], key=lambda i: recs[i]["bout"])
        if reading == "b_common":
            _, _, evc = apl.pca(np.vstack([progs[i].sdf[progs[i].ix_stim] for i in ix]))
            ds = [apl.n_pcs(evc, 0.8, "le80")] * 3
        else:
            ds = [apl.n_pcs(progs[i].ev, 0.8, "min80") for i in ix]
        PART[(reading, p)] = (np.array([apl.participation(progs[i].coeffs, progs[i].ev, d)[1] for i, d in zip(ix, ds)]), ds)
print({k: v[1] for k, v in PART.items()})

fig7f-strongly-variable-neurons¶

Neurons with high participation in one response often have low participation in another; every preparation contains neurons whose change in participation well exceeds that predicted by a noise model.

rows = []

    dP = np.column_stack([P[0] - P[1], P[1] - P[2], P[0] - P[2]])

    for pool in ["all_pairs", "consecutive"]:

halving-participation¶

Even the most strongly participating neurons in a response could more than halve their participation in other evoked responses.

In [38]:
rows = []
for (reading, p), (P, ds) in PART.items():
    for sel_name in ["top_neuron", "top_10pct"]:
        hit, examples = False, []
        for a in range(3):
            sel = [int(np.argmax(P[a]))] if sel_name == "top_neuron" else list(np.argsort(P[a])[::-1][:int(np.ceil(0.1 * P.shape[1]))])
            for b in range(3):
                if b == a:
                    continue
                lo = [n for n in sel if P[b][n] < 0.5 * P[a][n]]
                if lo:
                    hit = True
                    examples.append((a + 1, b + 1, len(lo), round(float(min(P[b][n] / P[a][n] for n in lo)), 3)))
        rows.append({"reading": reading, "selection": sel_name, "prep": p, "halves": hit, "examples": examples[:3]})
HV = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(HV.groupby(["reading", "selection"]).halves.sum().to_string())
print(HV[HV.reading == "a_own"].to_string(index=False))

fig7s1-rate-synchrony¶

A neuron's participation reflects both its firing rate and its synchrony; firing rate explains on average 50% of the variation in participation within a response, and rate changes 23% of the change in participation between responses.

In [39]:
rows = []
for reading in ["a_own", "b_common"]:
    for rate_from in [32.5, 30.0]:
        r2, dr2, dr2_code = [], [], []
        for p in range(1, 11):
            ix = sorted([i for i, r in enumerate(recs) if r["prep"] == p], key=lambda i: recs[i]["bout"])
            P = PART[(reading, p)][0]
            rates = np.array([[np.sum(tr >= rate_from) / (progs[i].t_end - rate_from) for tr in progs[i].trains] for i in ix])
            r2 += [np.corrcoef(P[b], rates[b])[0, 1] ** 2 for b in range(3)]
            dR = np.column_stack([rates[0] - rates[1], rates[0] - rates[2], rates[1] - rates[2]])
            dPm = np.column_stack([P[0] - P[1], P[0] - P[2], P[1] - P[2]])
            dPc = np.column_stack([P[0] - P[1], P[1] - P[2], P[0] - P[2]])
            dr2 += [np.corrcoef(dR[:, c], dPm[:, c])[0, 1] ** 2 for c in range(3)]
            dr2_code += [np.corrcoef(dR[:, c], dPc[:, c])[0, 1] ** 2 for c in range(3)]
        rows.append({"reading": reading, "rate_from_s": rate_from, "mean_R2_within": np.mean(r2), "range_within": f"{min(r2):.2f} to {max(r2):.2f}",
                     "mean_R2_change_matched": np.mean(dr2), "mean_R2_change_code_pairing": np.mean(dr2_code), "n_programs": len(r2), "n_pairs": len(dr2)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))

fig7gh-robust-to-participation¶

The distance between a pair of responses does not correlate with the total change in neuron participation between them nor with the distance between their participation distributions; the program is robust to the participation of single neurons.

# (b) the common count (at most 80% of the concatenated PCA), as in the Participation section.
PARTR = {}
for k in ["own/min80", "own/le80", "pooled/min80", "pooled/le80"]:

    for p in range(1, 11):

        _, _, evc = apl.pca(np.vstack([pg[i].sdf[pg[i].ix_stim] for i in ix]))
        for reading, ds in [("a_own", [apl.n_pcs(pg[i].ev, 0.8, rule) for i in ix]), ("b_common", [apl.n_pcs(evc, 0.8, "le80")] * 3)]:
            PARTR[(k, reading, p)] = np.array([apl.participation(pg[i].coeffs, pg[i].ev, d)[1] for i, d in zip(ix, ds)])

        T["norm_dist"] = T.H / T.ctrl_mean
        for reading in ["a_own", "b_common"]:
            tc, hd = [], []
            for row in T.itertuples():
                P = PARTR[(k, reading, row.prep)]
                i, j = [int(x) - 1 for x in row.pair.split(",")]
                tc.append(np.abs(P[i] - P[j]).sum())
                hd.append(apl.hellinger(P[i], P[j]))
            T["total_change"], T["hellinger"] = tc, hd
            keep = ~((T.prep == 4) & T.pair.isin(["1,2", "1,3"]))

                ck = T.norm_dist < 1

Result: partially reproduced, resting on the adopted reading. Under the adopted width and count, each set of distances finds one significant slope of two: with the recurrent points (Methods), the normalised distance rises with the total change in participation (slope 0.0127, p = 0.031, R-squared 0.17, 28 pairs) but not with the Hellinger distance (p = 0.35); with the code's point sets, it rises with the Hellinger distance (p = 0.028) but not with the total change (p = 0.11). Participation reading (b) gives the same pattern (p = 0.032 and 0.017). So one of the two absences holds and the other fails. Under own/le80 one slope is significant with the recurrent points (total change, p = 0.036) and none with the code's points (lowest p 0.053); under pooled/min80 and pooled/le80, with participation from the pooled width, no slope is significant with the legend's exclusion (lowest p 0.085 and 0.069). With the code's exclusion (pairs with normalised distance below 1, 29 pairs with the recurrent points), pooled/min80 has a significant total-change slope with the recurrent points (p = 0.028 and 0.029, participation readings (a) and (b)), and pooled/le80 has none (lowest p 0.069). The outcome depends on the reading, and under pooled/min80 on the exclusion rule.

fig7s2-no-invariant-core¶

No small invariant core of strongly participating, phasically active neurons, such as a classic central pattern generator, is found across preparations.

Ensembles by the code's consensus clustering of each program from stimulation onset, typed by the autocorrelogram of their pooled spikes against interval shuffles (port in apl.py, citing each MATLAB file). A neuron takes its ensemble's type; persistent neurons have the same type in all three programs. Participation is that of the Participation section (readings (a) and (b)). Run for the recording's own width (the code's Data.GaussSD, the adopted width) and the pooled width, each with two seeds.

def core_table(res, reading):
    out = []
    for p in range(1, 11):
        T3 = np.column_stack([o["types"] for o in sorted([o for o in res if o["prep"] == p], key=lambda o: o["bout"])])
        P = PART[(reading, p)][0]
        high, dmax = P.max(0), np.abs(np.column_stack([P[0] - P[1], P[1] - P[2]])).max(1)
        persist = {names[t]: int(np.all(T3 == t, 1).sum()) for t in names}
        osc = np.flatnonzero(np.all(T3 == 2, 1))
        if osc.size:
            upper = np.percentile(high[osc], 90, method="hazen")     # MATLAB prctile
            sel = osc[high[osc] > upper]
        else:
            sel = osc
        med = float(np.median(dmax[sel])) if sel.size else np.nan
        top_all = np.argsort(high)[::-1][:int(np.ceil(0.1 * high.size))]
        out.append({"prep": p, "neurons": high.size, **{f"persistent_{k}": v for k, v in persist.items()},
                    "top10pct_osc_n": int(sel.size), "top_osc_median_maxP": float(np.median(high[sel])) if sel.size else np.nan,
                    "top_osc_median_max_change": med, "core": bool(med < 0.1),
                    "no_typing_top10pct_median_max_change": float(np.median(dmax[top_all]))})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

Result: reproduced. With the port of the code's ensemble toolbox, every preparation has neurons typed oscillator in all three programs (16 to 84 per preparation, adopted width and seed), and the top 10% of them by maximum participation have a median maximum change between consecutive programs of 0.068 to 0.440 of the program maximum. Only preparation 2 has an invariant core by the claims file's rule (median change 0.068, under 0.1); 1 of 10 preparations, fewer than half, under the adopted width with seed 7, and 0 or 1 of 10 under both widths, both seeds and both readings of participation. The top 10% of persistent oscillators holds 2 to 8 neurons per preparation. Without typing, the top 10% of all neurons by maximum participation have median maximum changes of 0.12 to 0.32, under 0.1 in no preparation. The legend's statement that only the oscillator class had a consistently typed neuron in all ten preparations holds in part: oscillators persist in 10 of 10 preparations under every variant, but persistent bursters are found in 6 to 10 preparations (10 in one variant), persistent tonic neurons in 2 or 3 and persistent pausers in none. The clustering is random (k-means starts); two seeds are shown, and the port has not been checked against MATLAB's output.

fig8-caudolateral¶

Neurons with strong participation across the three responses, and those with highly variable participation, lie mainly in the caudo-lateral quadrant of the ganglion.

Blocked (see the header): neither the data set, its documentation nor the paper's text says which directions of the array's x and y axes are caudal and lateral. The counts by quadrant of the array coordinates are shown so that the claim can be judged once the orientation is known, with true quintiles as the criterion's variant, and the share of the top fifth in its most common quadrant against the share of all neurons there; they decide nothing here.

    for p in group:
        P = PART[("a_own", p)][0]
        vals_max.append(P.max(0)); vals_rng.append(P.max(0) - P.min(0))
        xs.append(D["coords"][p - 1]["x"]); ys.append(D["coords"][p - 1]["y"])
    allmax = np.concatenate([PART[("a_own", p)][0].max(0) for p in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10]])
    allrng = np.concatenate([np.ptp(PART[("a_own", p)][0], 0) for p in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10]])
    x, y = np.concatenate(xs), np.concatenate(ys)
    cx, cy = 25.0, 25.0     # centre of the 501 x 501 template, in coordinate units
    q = np.where(x >= cx, "x+", "x-").astype(object) + np.where(y >= cy, "y+", "y-")
    for name, v, allv in [("max", np.concatenate(vals_max), allmax), ("range", np.concatenate(vals_rng), allrng)]:
        edges = np.linspace(allv.min(), allv.max(), 6)
        for division, top in [("equal-width fifth (code)", v >= edges[-2]), ("true quintile (variant)", v >= np.quantile(v, 0.8))]:
            counts = pd.Series(q[top]).value_counts()
            rows.append({"side": side, "measure": name, "division": division, "neurons": v.size, "top_fifth": int(top.sum()),
                         "by_quadrant": counts.to_dict(), "largest_quadrant": counts.index[0] if top.any() else None,
                         "largest_share": round(counts.iloc[0] / top.sum(), 2) if top.any() else np.nan,
                         "all_neurons_in_that_quadrant": round(float(np.mean(q == counts.index[0])), 2) if top.any() else np.nan})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Result: blocked, metadata insufficient (see the header). Shown for the verifier, not judged: in each side the top-fifth neurons concentrate in one quadrant of the array coordinates, the same quadrant for maximum under both divisions and for range under true quintiles (left x-y-, right x-y+). Under true quintiles that quadrant holds 34% to 41% of the top fifth against 19% to 20% of all neurons; under the code's equal-width fifths 71% (left, maximum, 15 of 21) and 54% (right, 15 of 28). The code's equal-width division leaves only 1 or 2 neurons in the top fifth of the range, so that half of the test is nearly empty as the code defines it. Which anatomical quadrant these are cannot be told without the array's orientation.

No reading makes all of these hold. The adopted reading follows the Methods' count and the recording's own median ISI; the outcomes that rest on it are marked as assumed.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. It is a Python port of the paper's MATLAB code, following the Methods where they fix a detail and the code where they do not. The Methods' kernel width as printed gives 21 to 76 dimensions (33 to 76 with median ISI / 12, 21 to 41 with / sqrt(12)), and the analysis uses the code's width (the median ISI) for everything after claim fig2b. The code computes that median over the recordings of the same bout number read so far; the adopted reading uses the recording's own. The number of PCs is the smallest reaching 80% (Methods) in the adopted reading; the code's rule (at most 80%) is run alongside and changes some outcomes (table above). A window counts as coalesced or recurrent at at least 90% of its points, as the Methods say. The local models use the contiguous run of neighbours as the Methods describe. The permutation test of fig5b permutes the delays against time (10000 permutations); the code's test is shown too. The decoding uses a numpy IRLS for MATLAB's glmfit; the 90% models use the full history grid under the two readings with the recording's own width and four histories under pooled/le80. The ensembles and types of fig7s2 come from a Python port of the code's consensus clustering and autocorrelogram typing, with Lloyd's k-means for MATLAB's kmeans, not checked against MATLAB's output.

What was found about the data set. The files match their checksums and the description: 30 recordings of 75 to 160 neurons, 1131 in all, P10 for nine, coordinates for all ten preparations. The paper's 120 to 180 neurons per recording cannot be right with its own total of 1131. The P10 sampling (1629.7 Hz) agrees with the description's 1630 Hz, not the paper's 1600 Hz. The P10 file names of preparation 2 drop the "B" of its spike file. The coordinates have no unit and no orientation, so which part of the array is caudo-lateral cannot be told from the data set.
